dok_rationale: Part (c) requires judging two competing interval reports by coordinating recruitment, numerical conditions, and interval width, then explaining why the more precise-looking output cannot support the target-population claim.
stem: A library system has 20,000 adult cardholders and wants to estimate $p$, the proportion who used a digital audiobook last month.\par\smallskip \textbf{Plan A:} A computer takes an SRS of 200 cardholder IDs. All answer; 116 say yes.\par \textbf{Plan B:} A newsletter link lets cardholders choose to respond once. Of 800 respondents, 520 say yes.\par\smallskip \textbf{Eli:} ``Use Plan B. Its larger sample gives the narrower interval.''\par \textbf{Dana:} ``Use Plan A. Entry into the sample matters more than the narrowest output.''
first_take: Which plan, if either, should estimate all adult cardholders? Cite one collection detail.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Define the population parameter $p$ in context and name the confidence-interval procedure that would be appropriate when its conditions are met.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: For each plan, compute $\hat p$, check the random, 10 percent, and large-count conditions, and calculate the 95 percent formula interval. Mark any nondefensible population interval.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Decide which plan can support a 95 percent interval for all cardholders. Cite recruitment and a numerical condition, compare interval widths, and explain the reader consequence of reporting Plan B's output.

answers.a: Here $p$ is the proportion of all 20,000 adult library cardholders who used a digital audiobook last month. When conditions are met, the procedure is a one-sample $z$-interval for a population proportion.
answers.b: Plan A has $\hat p=116/200=0.58$. It is an SRS; $200\le0.10(20{,}000)=2{,}000$; and counts are 116 and 84. Thus $SE=0.0348999$, $ME=1.96(SE)=0.0684037$, and the valid interval is $(0.5116,0.6484)$. Plan B has $\hat p=520/800=0.65$; $800\le2{,}000$ and counts 520 and 280 pass, but self-selection fails the random condition. Its mechanical output is $0.65\pm0.0330523$, or $(0.6169,0.6831)$, not a defensible population confidence interval.
answers.c: Use Plan A. Its SRS, $200\le2{,}000$, and counts 116 and 84 support the interval $(0.512,0.648)$ for all cardholders. Its width is about $0.1368$ versus Plan B's smaller formula width, $0.0661$. Plan B's volunteers may differ systematically from nonrespondents; its margin of error covers random variation, not self-selection. Reporting it would falsely suggest that a narrow range represents all cardholders with 95 percent confidence.

expectedElements.description: Chooses Plan A for population inference
Cites the SRS and one numerical check
Notes $0.066<0.137$ but Plan B is nonrandom

scoringGuide.E: Chooses A, cites both kinds of checks, contrasts widths, and explains self-selection.
scoringGuide.P: Chooses A but omits a check, width, or reader consequence.
scoringGuide.I: Chooses B for size or width, or treats numerical checks as randomness.
